ai.title: Multiple Choice Questions in Biochemistry & Genetics
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Learn how to approach biochemistry and genetics MCQs clinically, using a bedside reasoning framework. Focus on common tropical conditions, limited investigations, and exam‑style strategies.

sections.p: Multiple choice questions (MCQs) test applied knowledge. In low‑resource settings, examiners expect you to link biochemical pathways to common diseases and to think about what you would do if tests are unavailable.
b: Each question has one best answer among five options.
Clinical reasoning beats memorisation.

sections.p: Read the stem, identify the clinical scenario, then map the biochemistry/genetics clue to a disease or management step.
b: Spot keywords: ‘elevated’, ‘deficiency’, ‘inheritance’, ‘drug‑induced’.
Eliminate implausible answers by checking consistency with epidemiology and resource limits.

sections.p: Key enzymes are often regulated by feedback inhibition, hormones, or co‑factor availability. Recognise which regulator is altered in the scenario.
b: Hormonal control (insulin, cortisol) is common in diabetes and stress‑related disorders.
Co‑factor deficiency (vitamin B12, folate) is frequent in malnutrition and HIV patients.

sections.p: Pathology arises from enzyme defects, gene mutations, or toxic inhibition. Prioritise causes that are prevalent in East Africa.
b: Inherited enzyme deficiencies: sickle‑cell disease (HbS), G6PD deficiency.
Acquired defects: malaria‑induced hemolysis, TB drug‑induced hepatotoxicity.

sections.p: Link the biochemical abnormality to the patient’s presentation, prognosis and immediate management.
b: Elevated lactate → tissue hypoxia, severe malaria, septic shock.
Low serum folate → macrocytic anaemia, teratogenic risk in pregnancy.

t.b: Is the electrolyte disturbance causing the presenting symptom? → Guides replacement or avoidance of offending drugs.
Is hemolysis due to malaria? → If unavailable, use clinical malaria score and treat empirically.
Is macrocytosis due to B12 deficiency? → If assay unavailable, assess dietary risk and neurological signs.
Does the patient have a hereditary hemoglobinopathy? → If not possible, use family history and peripheral smear clues.

sections.p: Treat the underlying biochemical derangement, then provide supportive care.
b: Folate supplementation for deficiency – safe, inexpensive.
Avoid drugs that inhibit CYP450 when a patient has reduced metabolism (e.g., isoniazid in TB).
In G6PD deficiency, stop oxidant drugs (primaquine) and give supportive transfusion if severe.

sections.p: Biochemistry questions may look like pure laboratory queries but actually test clinical decision‑making.
b: Distinguish ‘elevated creatine kinase’ from ‘muscle breakdown due to malaria’.
Separate ‘genetic predisposition to hypertension’ from ‘secondary hypertension from renal disease’.

sections.p: In low‑resource labs, values may be falsely normal.
b: Serum bilirubin can be low despite severe hemolysis if measured after transfusion.
Rapid HIV tests may be negative early; consider repeat testing if suspicion remains.

sections.p: Strategic tips for MCQs in biochemistry & genetics.
b: Always link the biochemical change to a clinical picture before choosing an answer.
Eliminate options that are impossible in the local epidemiology.
If a test is not mentioned, assume it is unavailable and think of bedside alternatives.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe metabolic acidosis with altered mental status
Unexplained rapid deterioration after starting antiretroviral therapy
Acute hemolysis with jaundice in a known G6PD‑deficient patient

faq.q: How do I guess the answer when I’m unsure?
faq.a: Look for the option that best fits the patient’s context, epidemiology and the most likely pathophysiology.

faq.q: What if the question mentions a test I cannot perform here?
faq.a: Choose the answer that reflects a clinical alternative or empirical treatment appropriate for low‑resource settings.
Focus on the function, regulation and diseases associated with the enzyme rather than rote memorisation.

exam: A 6‑year‑old with severe malaria has a high lactate – what does this indicate and how does it change management? — Indicates tissue hypoxia; start aggressive fluid resuscitation and consider exchange transfusion if lactate >5 mmol/L.

A pregnant woman on zidovudine presents with macrocytic anaemia – which deficiency is most likely and why? — Folate deficiency, because zidovudine interferes with folate metabolism and pregnancy increases demand.

A patient with sickle‑cell disease develops jaundice after taking primaquine – what is the mechanism and next step? — Oxidative stress triggers hemolysis in G6PD deficiency; stop primaquine and give supportive care.
You see a peripheral smear with bite cells in a malaria‑endemic area – what biochemical defect should you suspect? — G6PD deficiency causing impaired NADPH regeneration.

Elevated serum transaminases are found in a TB patient on isoniazid – how do you decide whether to continue therapy? — Assess degree of rise; if <5 × ULN and patient is asymptomatic, continue with monitoring.

A child with failure to thrive has low serum B12 but the lab is unavailable – what bedside clues support the diagnosis? — Neurological signs (paresthesia), macrocytosis on CBC, dietary history of low animal protein.

Which enzyme deficiency explains the accumulation of phenylalanine in a newborn from a low‑resource clinic? — Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency (PKU), consider dietary restriction of phenylalanine.
A patient on rifampicin develops orange urine – what does this indicate and does it require treatment? — Rifampicin excretion; benign, no treatment needed.
